title: Neurodegenerative diseases and brain cancers
summary: Neurodegenerative diseases and brain cancers today represent one of the greatest challenges of modern medicine. Long explained by cell theory, they are now revealing another face: that of the mitochondria, true regulators of metabolic health. This booklet explores the mitocentric avenue, showing how fasting, deep rest and sleep can restore energy flexibility and protect the brain. At the crossroads of scientific research and hypotoxic nutrition, it proposes an integrative approach in which conventional medicine and metabolic strategies complement each other. It is an invitation to rethink brain health as a global restoration of the biological terrain, in the service of prevention and healing.

blocks.text: Foreword

Neurodegenerative diseases and brain cancers are today one of the greatest challenges of modern medicine. Their rising incidence, linked to population aging, longer life expectancy and contemporary lifestyles, calls for new thinking about their underlying causes. For nearly two centuries, medicine relied on a cellular approach: the cell was considered the fundamental unit of life and, consequently, the seat of pathological dysfunction. Thus, in Alzheimer’s disease, attention focused on neuronal degeneration and the accumulation of amyloid plaques; in Parkinson’s disease, on the loss of dopaminergic neurons; in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), on the degeneration of motor neurons; and in glioblastoma, on the uncontrolled proliferation of tumor cells.

Yet over the past thirty years or so, a paradigm shift has been under way. Mitochondria, long reduced to the role of “power plants,” now appear as essential regulators of metabolic health. They influence gene expression, coordinate cellular processes and determine the body’s ability to adapt to changes in the environment. Dr. Matthew Phillips, a neurologist and researcher, proposes a mitocentric reading of neurodegenerative diseases and brain cancers: insulin resistance, far from being a primary cause, is seen as a protective response to chronic carbohydrate assault. In other words, the body sets up insulin resistance to protect its mitochondria from an excess of glucose, a veritable dietary “onslaught” that generates free radicals and oxidative damage.

This perspective echoes the work of researchers such as Jean Seignalet, who highlighted the impact of diet on autoimmune and degenerative diseases, and Dale Bredesen, who showed that multimodal protocols could reverse some early cases of Alzheimer’s. It is also in keeping with the Family Clinic philosophy: putting nutrition, rest and metabolic flexibility back at the heart of prevention and care.

From this standpoint, health can no longer be viewed solely as the correction of symptoms with medication. It must be understood as a state of dynamic balance, in which the body is able to switch between different fuels (glucose, ketone bodies, lactate) as needed. This energy flexibility is the key to neuronal resilience. To function properly, neurons must be able to shift from a glycolytic mode to a ketogenic mode, and back again, without blockage or overload.

Dr. Phillips emphasizes three “subtractive” pillars: intermittent fasting, deep rest and optimized sleep. These practices, often neglected in favor of “additive” strategies (adding supplements, increasing exercise, multiplying interventions), reduce the metabolic load and restore the mitochondria’s capacity to adapt. They are consistent with the clinical observations of Palmblad and Kjeldsen-Kragh, who showed that fasting could improve polyarthritis by reducing systemic inflammation, confirming the global effect of metabolic strategies.

This booklet offers a synthesis of these approaches, linking the findings of contemporary research with the principles of hypotoxic nutrition and integrative health strategies. The aim is twofold: to give patients and practitioners a clear understanding of the mechanisms at work, and to suggest concrete ways to strengthen mitochondrial and metabolic resilience.

The point is not to set conventional medicine against metabolic approaches, but to integrate them. Medications, used wisely, can improve quality of life and reduce symptoms. But they are not enough to halt the disease process. Metabolic strategies, on the other hand, aim to restore the terrain, reduce chronic inflammation, improve energy flexibility and strengthen mitochondrial resilience. Together, they can offer a more complete and more lasting approach.

This paradigm shift is reminiscent of the great scientific revolutions: Semmelweis, who demonstrated the importance of handwashing, was long rejected before being recognized; Harvey, who described the circulation of the blood, was accused of heresy before his model became self-evident. In the same way, it is likely that in a few decades the mitocentric view will come to be seen as self-evident, relegating cell theory to the status of a historical stage.

This booklet follows on from the books Cooking to Heal (2026) and 100 Hypotoxic Recipes for Every Day, offering an integrated, scientific and practical approach. It is an invitation to rethink brain and metabolic health, not as a fight against isolated symptoms, but as a global restoration of the biological terrain.
Cell theory vs. mitocentric theory

Cell theory, formulated in the nineteenth century, dominated biological and medical thinking for nearly two centuries. It rests on the idea that the cell is the fundamental unit of life and that diseases result from cellular dysfunction. This approach made considerable advances possible: understanding of cell division, identification of the mechanisms of mutation, development of chemotherapy and targeted therapies. In the case of neurodegenerative diseases, it steered research toward the study of neurons and their alterations: amyloid deposits and synaptic degeneration in Alzheimer’s, loss of dopaminergic neurons in Parkinson’s, motor neuron damage in ALS. In the case of brain cancers, it led to the analysis of the uncontrolled proliferation of tumor cells, their ability to escape apoptosis and to invade neighboring tissues.

However, this approach has its limits. By focusing on the cell, it overlooks the role of intracellular structures, in particular the mitochondria. Discovered late, these were relegated to the rank of mere ATP producers. Yet recent research shows that they are involved in regulating apoptosis, modulating immunity, managing oxidative stress and gene expression. They appear to be the true conductors of metabolism. Their dysfunction is now recognized as a major factor in aging, neuronal degeneration and carcinogenesis.

The mitocentric theory therefore proposes a reversal of perspective: the cell would be merely an infrastructure serving the mitochondria, which would be the true units of life. This view echoes the terrain theory championed by Antoine Béchamp, as opposed to Louis Pasteur’s germ theory. Béchamp held that disease resulted from an imbalance in the biological terrain rather than from an external attack. For lack of solid evidence in his day, his ideas were marginalized. Today, they are finding new resonance thanks to discoveries about the central role of the mitochondria.

This paradigm shift is reminiscent of the great scientific revolutions. Semmelweis, who demonstrated the importance of handwashing, was long rejected before being recognized. Harvey, who described the circulation of the blood, was accused of heresy before his model became self-evident. In the same way, it is likely that in a few decades the mitocentric view will come to be seen as self-evident, relegating cell theory to the status of a historical stage.

Dr. Matthew Phillips stresses that insulin resistance, often considered a disease in its own right, is in reality only a protective response to chronic carbohydrate assault. The mitochondria, saturated by excess glucose, produce free radicals in excess and suffer damage. The body then sets up insulin resistance to limit the entry of glucose into cells and protect the mitochondria. This mitocentric reading makes it possible to link apparently different conditions (Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, ALS, glioblastoma) to one and the same fundamental mechanism: mitochondrial failure.

Thus the mitocentric theory does not deny the contributions of cell theory, but goes beyond them. It offers an integrative vision in which health is defined by the ability of the mitochondria to maintain energy balance and to adapt to changes in the environment. It opens the way to new therapeutic strategies centered on restoring metabolic flexibility and reducing oxidative stress.
Metabolism and energy flexibility

Human health can be seen as a dynamic balance between two opposing but complementary forces: anabolism, which builds and stores, and catabolism, which breaks down and recycles. This balance is particularly crucial in the brain, an organ whose energy consumption is disproportionate to its mass. To function properly, neurons need a metabolic flexibility that allows them to switch between different fuels according to needs and circumstances.

Traditionally, glucose has been considered the brain’s main fuel. Indeed, it circulates abundantly in the blood and readily enters neurons thanks to specific transporters. However, this exclusive dependence on glucose has its limits. In cases of chronic excess, as with diets rich in rapidly absorbed sugars and refined starches, the mitochondria are subjected to oxidative overload. They then produce free radicals in excess, which damages membranes, proteins and mitochondrial DNA. This oxidative stress is now recognized as a major factor in neuronal aging and degeneration.

Conversely, during fasting or carbohydrate restriction, the body mobilizes ketone bodies (beta-hydroxybutyrate, acetoacetate), derived from the breakdown of fatty acids. These molecules are a cleaner source of energy: they generate fewer free radicals and promote the expression of protective genes. Several studies, including those of Palmblad and Kjeldsen-Kragh on therapeutic fasting, have shown that this metabolic switch could reduce systemic inflammation and improve cellular function. In the neurological context, ketone bodies improve synaptic function, reduce excitotoxicity and promote neurogenesis.

Dr. Matthew Phillips stresses the importance of not getting stuck in a single energy mode. Being in permanent glycolysis (continuously high glucose) is harmful, but remaining in strict ketosis without alternation can also be a problem. The ideal is to develop energy flexibility, that is, the ability to switch between glucose, ketones and lactate as needed. Lactate, long regarded as a mere metabolic waste product, is now recognized as a valuable brain fuel, especially during physical exercise.

This energy flexibility is comparable to a hybrid engine able to run on several fuels. A flexible brain can use glucose during intense effort, switch to ketones during fasting, and draw on lactate during physical activity. This adaptability confers resilience in the face of metabolic stress and reduces the risk of degeneration.
Strategies to restore this flexibility include:

items: Intermittent fasting: reduces the carbohydrate load and activates ketone production.
Cyclical ketogenic diet: promotes adaptation to ketones while maintaining the ability to use glucose.
Moderate physical exercise: stimulates the use of lactate and improves insulin sensitivity.
Hypotoxic nutrition (Seignalet, Family Clinic): reduces chronic inflammation and protects the mitochondria.

It is also in keeping with the Family Clinic philosophy, which emphasizes restoring the biological terrain through simple, daily and integrative strategies.

Ultimately, brain health cannot be reduced to the correction of isolated symptoms. It must be understood as the body’s ability to maintain energy flexibility and mitochondrial resilience. It is this adaptability that allows neurons to withstand assaults, regenerate and maintain their cognitive and motor functions.
The three subtractive pillars: fasting, deep rest and sleep

In contemporary medicine, the emphasis is often on so-called “additive” strategies: adding a medication, increasing the number of exercise sessions, enriching the diet with supplements, intensifying therapeutic interventions. This additive logic, deeply rooted in medical culture, rests on the idea that health is built by accumulating means of action. Yet Dr. Matthew Phillips reminds us that, to regain its balance, the body sometimes needs the opposite: to subtract. Removing excesses, reducing assaults, offering metabolic breaks. It is from this perspective that the three subtractive pillars arise: intermittent fasting, deep rest and optimized sleep.
Intermittent fasting

Intermittent fasting consists of alternating periods of eating with periods of voluntary abstention from food. Unlike restrictive diets, it does not aim to reduce calories permanently, but to establish cycles of metabolic rest. During these fasting periods, the body switches to using ketone bodies, which reduces the production of free radicals and promotes autophagy, a process of cellular cleanup.
The benefits of intermittent fasting are many:

items: Reduced inflammation: by lowering the carbohydrate load, fasting reduces pro-inflammatory cytokines.
Mitochondrial protection: ketones produce cleaner energy and activate longevity genes.
Improved insulin sensitivity: periods without food intake allow the receptors to regenerate.
Cognitive stimulation: several studies show improved mental clarity and memory.

blocks.text: As early as the 1990s, Palmblad and Kjeldsen-Kragh demonstrated that fasting could improve polyarthritis by reducing systemic inflammation. These results, transposed to the neurological field, suggest that intermittent fasting could slow the progression of neurodegenerative diseases by reducing oxidative stress and promoting energy flexibility.
Deep rest

Deep rest is not the same as sleep. It consists of moments of conscious relaxation, relaxation practices or meditation that help reduce chronic stress. By constantly activating the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, stress leads to excessive cortisol production. When chronically elevated, cortisol damages neurons, reduces neurogenesis and promotes degeneration.
Deep rest techniques include:

items: Conscious breathing: slowing the breathing rate to activate the parasympathetic system.
Mindfulness meditation: reducing mental activity and promoting emotional regulation.
Progressive muscle relaxation: releasing bodily tension to calm the nervous system.
Short naps: giving the brain restorative breaks without entering deep sleep.

blocks.text: These practices, often seen as optional extras, are in fact essential. They reduce the allostatic load, that is, the cumulative wear and tear caused by chronic stress. By restoring a state of calm, they promote mitochondrial regeneration and improve neuronal resilience.
Optimized sleep

Sleep is an active process of regeneration. During the night, the body activates cellular repair mechanisms, consolidates memory and regulates hormones. Deep sleep promotes the removal of metabolic waste via the glymphatic system, in particular the beta-amyloid proteins implicated in Alzheimer’s.
Optimized sleep involves:

items: Regular hours: going to bed and getting up at set times to synchronize the circadian clock.
Quality of the environment: darkness, quiet, a suitable temperature.
Less screen time: avoiding blue light, which disrupts melatonin secretion.
Calming rituals: reading, meditation, breathing exercises before bed.

blocks.text: Sleep disorders are common in neurodegenerative diseases. They worsen degeneration by reducing the capacity for neuronal repair. Restoring good-quality sleep is therefore a therapeutic priority.
A synergy of the three pillars
These three pillars should not be considered in isolation. Their effectiveness lies in their synergy:

items: Intermittent fasting reduces the metabolic load and promotes ketosis.
Deep rest lowers stress and protects neurons.
Optimized sleep regenerates and clears waste.

blocks.text: Together, they give the body restorative breaks, reduce chronic assaults and restore energy flexibility. They form a solid foundation for any strategy to prevent or treat neurodegenerative diseases and brain cancers.
Metabolic risk factors

Neurodegenerative diseases and brain cancers do not arise in a biological vacuum. They develop on a pathological terrain marked by chronic metabolic imbalances. Dr. Matthew Phillips emphasizes that the majority of the patients he sees have poor metabolic health, characterized by a set of risk factors that, far from being independent, interact and reinforce one another. Understanding these factors is essential in order to prevent, slow or manage the course of neurological and oncological diseases.
Abdominal obesity

Obesity, and abdominal obesity in particular, is a central marker of metabolic syndrome. Excess visceral fat is not simply passive storage: it is an active endocrine tissue that secretes pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6) and adipokines that disrupt insulin sensitivity. This chronic low-grade inflammation contributes to insulin resistance, oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction. In the brain, it promotes neuroinflammation, impairs synaptic plasticity and accelerates degeneration.
Insulin resistance and diabetes

Insulin resistance is often perceived as a disease in itself. Dr. Phillips points out that it is in reality a protective response: the body limits the entry of glucose into cells to protect the mitochondria from overload. However, when this resistance becomes chronic, it leads to persistent hyperglycemia, which damages blood vessels, promotes protein glycation and heightens oxidative stress. Type 2 diabetes, the ultimate consequence of this resistance, is strongly associated with an increased risk of dementia, stroke and cancer.
High blood pressure

Hypertension is another pillar of metabolic syndrome. It often results from vascular stiffness linked to inflammation and oxidative stress. In the brain, it promotes vascular micro-lesions, reduces neuronal perfusion and increases the risk of vascular dementia. It acts in synergy with insulin resistance and obesity to create a terrain conducive to degeneration.
Lipid abnormalities

In contrast to the traditional focus on LDL cholesterol, Dr. Phillips stresses the importance of triglycerides and HDL as relevant markers of metabolic syndrome. High triglycerides and low HDL signal poor metabolic health. These abnormalities reflect the body’s inability to handle fats properly, which leads to liver overload, steatosis and impaired energy flexibility. In the brain, they promote the accumulation of toxic lipids and disrupt synaptic function.
Associated comorbidities

Metabolic syndrome is not limited to its classic criteria. It is often accompanied by comorbidities such as non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, a true reflection of carbohydrate and fat overload. This liver involvement reflects the body’s inability to cope with excess energy and is a major risk marker for neurological diseases. Other comorbidities include sleep apnea, hyperuricemia and thyroid disorders, which worsen the metabolic terrain.
An integrative reading of the risks

Dr. Phillips stresses that these factors are not independent of neurological diseases. They are not simply “associated diseases,” but take a direct part in the disease process. Obesity, insulin resistance, hypertension and lipid abnormalities create an inflammatory and oxidative terrain that weakens neurons and mitochondria. From this perspective, treating these factors is not a secondary option but a therapeutic priority.
Empowerment and prevention

One of Dr. Phillips’s key messages is the importance of patient empowerment. By identifying their metabolic risk factors, patients come to realize that their neurological health is not determined solely by irreversible processes, but can be influenced by their daily choices. Changing their diet, practicing intermittent fasting, establishing rest and sleep routines, adopting suitable physical activity: these are all levers that can improve metabolic health and, in turn, brain health.

This approach is in line with the Family Clinic philosophy: putting hypotoxic nutrition, energy flexibility and management of the terrain back at the heart of prevention. It is part of an integrative vision in which conventional medicine and metabolic strategies complement each other. Medications can reduce symptoms, but only a restoration of the metabolic terrain can offer lasting improvement.
Combined therapeutic approaches

Modern medicine relies largely on pharmacological treatments and technical interventions. In the field of neurodegenerative diseases and brain cancers, these approaches have brought notable advances: slower progression of symptoms, improved quality of life, longer survival. However, they have their limits. Medications, however effective they may be at reducing clinical manifestations, fail to halt the underlying disease process. Dr. Matthew Phillips points out that the majority of patients come back to the hospital a few months or years later, because the disease continues to progress despite treatment.

It is in this context that the idea of therapeutic integration emerges: combining the contributions of conventional medicine with metabolic and mitochondrial strategies. This approach is not about setting two visions against each other, but about bringing them together to offer the patient more complete and more lasting care.
Conventional medicine: a symptomatic role
Current medications mainly aim to reduce symptoms:

items: In Alzheimer’s, cholinesterase inhibitors temporarily improve memory.
In Parkinson’s, L-dopa compensates for the loss of dopamine.
In ALS, some treatments slightly slow progression.
In glioblastoma, surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy reduce the tumor mass.

blocks.text: These interventions are useful, sometimes indispensable, but they do not tackle the root of the problem. They are stopgaps, temporary solutions that improve quality of life without changing the pathological terrain.
Metabolic strategies: restoring the terrain
Metabolic approaches aim to strengthen mitochondrial resilience and restore energy flexibility. They include:

items: Intermittent fasting and calorie restriction protocols: reduce the carbohydrate load, activate autophagy and promote ketosis.
Adapted ketogenic diets: provide ketone bodies as an alternative fuel, reducing oxidative stress.
Hypotoxic nutrition (Seignalet, Family Clinic): eliminates pro-inflammatory foods and favors a diet rich in plants, quality oils and suitable proteins.
Moderate, regular physical exercise: improves insulin sensitivity, stimulates the use of lactate and promotes neurogenesis.
Deep rest and stress management: reduce chronic cortisol production, protect neurons and improve mitochondrial regeneration.
Optimized sleep: promotes the removal of metabolic waste and the consolidation of memory.

blocks.text: These strategies, often regarded as “optional extras” by conventional medicine, are in fact essential. They directly address the root causes of degeneration: carbohydrate overload, chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, metabolic rigidity.
Integrating the two approaches
Dr. Phillips proposes a clear hierarchy:

items: The A-game must be metabolic. Strategies that act on the terrain form the foundation of health.
The B-game must be pharmacological. Medications play a supporting role, improving quality of life and reducing symptoms.

blocks.text: This integration avoids two pitfalls:

items: The all-medication approach, which masks symptoms without restoring the terrain.
The all-natural approach, which neglects the contribution of conventional treatments in certain critical situations.

blocks.text: In practice, this means that the patient receives comprehensive care: suitable drug treatment to reduce symptoms, combined with a metabolic protocol aimed at restoring mitochondrial health.
Deprescribing and therapeutic restraint

Another essential aspect is deprescribing. Doctors, out of reflex, often add medications when faced with a new symptom. This additive logic leads to polypharmacy, a source of side effects and complications. Dr. Phillips points out that many patients are hospitalized not because of their disease, but because of the adverse effects of their medications.

Deprescribing consists of gradually reducing unnecessary or harmful treatments, while giving priority to metabolic strategies. It reflects a logic of therapeutic restraint: using the right drug, at the right dose, for the right length of time, and only when necessary.
Toward integrative medicine

This combined approach echoes the work of Dale Bredesen, who showed that multimodal protocols could reverse some early cases of Alzheimer’s. It is also in keeping with the Family Clinic philosophy, which emphasizes restoring the biological terrain through simple, daily and integrative strategies.

Ultimately, the medicine of tomorrow will be neither exclusively pharmacological nor exclusively metabolic. It will be integrative, bringing together the contributions of both visions to offer the patient comprehensive care. Medications will remain useful, but they will be regarded as temporary tools, while metabolic strategies will form the foundation of lasting health.
General conclusion

Neurodegenerative diseases and brain cancers represent a major medical and human challenge. Their biological complexity, their often relentless progression and their impact on patients’ quality of life call for deep reflection on our therapeutic paradigms. For a long time, medicine relied on a cellular view: the cell as the fundamental unit of life, and disease as the consequence of cellular dysfunction. This approach made considerable advances possible, but today it is showing its limits.

Dr. Matthew Phillips and other researchers propose a mitocentric reading: the mitochondria, long reduced to the role of mere “power plants,” appear as the true regulators of health. They influence gene expression, coordinate cellular processes and determine the body’s ability to adapt to changes in the environment. Their dysfunction lies at the heart of neurodegenerative diseases and brain cancers.

This view echoes the terrain theory championed by Antoine Béchamp, who held that disease resulted from an imbalance in the biological terrain rather than from an external attack. For lack of solid evidence in his day, his ideas were marginalized. Today, they are finding new resonance thanks to discoveries about the central role of the mitochondria.

The conclusion that emerges is clear: health can no longer be viewed solely as the correction of symptoms with medication. It must be understood as a state of dynamic balance, in which the body is able to switch between different fuels (glucose, ketone bodies, lactate) as needed. This energy flexibility is the key to neuronal resilience. To function properly, neurons must be able to shift from a glycolytic mode to a ketogenic mode, and back again, without blockage or overload.

The three subtractive pillars—intermittent fasting, deep rest and optimized sleep—are simple but powerful strategies for restoring this balance. They reduce the metabolic load, protect the mitochondria and promote neuronal regeneration. Combined with hypotoxic nutrition, suitable physical activity and stress management, they offer an integrative approach to health.

Conventional medicine retains an important role, particularly in reducing symptoms and improving quality of life. But it must be integrated into a broader strategy centered on restoring the metabolic terrain. Medications should be regarded as temporary tools, while metabolic strategies form the foundation of lasting health.

This paradigm shift is reminiscent of the great scientific revolutions. Semmelweis, who demonstrated the importance of handwashing, was long rejected before being recognized. Harvey, who described the circulation of the blood, was accused of heresy before his model became self-evident. In the same way, it is likely that in a few decades the mitocentric view will come to be seen as self-evident, relegating cell theory to the status of a historical stage.
The general conclusion of this booklet is therefore a call to action:

items: For patients, to become aware that their neurological health is not determined solely by irreversible processes, but can be influenced by their daily choices.
For practitioners, to integrate metabolic strategies into their practice, alongside conventional treatments.
For research, to develop rigorous clinical trials to validate the effectiveness of metabolic and mitochondrial approaches.

Annotated bibliography and an opening toward the Family Clinic protocol

Our understanding of neurodegenerative diseases and brain cancers rests on an accumulation of knowledge from diverse disciplines: neurology, oncology, nutrition, cell biology and, more recently, mitochondrial biology. This booklet draws on several major references, which we present here as an annotated bibliography, in order to situate each author’s contributions and open onto the Family Clinic protocol.
Matthew Phillips – The Hidden Root Cause of Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s & Brain Cancer (2025)

Dr. Phillips is one of the pioneers of the mitocentric approach applied to neurological and oncological diseases. His work highlights the central role of mitochondria in metabolic health and proposes a new reading of insulin resistance as a protective mechanism. He stresses the importance of subtractive strategies (fasting, rest, sleep) and the need to restore energy flexibility. His clinical research, though preliminary, paves the way for an integrative medicine in which metabolic approaches form the foundation of health.
Jean Seignalet – L’alimentation ou la troisième médecine (Diet, or the Third Medicine, 2004)

Seignalet developed the concept of hypotoxic nutrition, based on eliminating pro-inflammatory foods (dairy products, modern cereals, excessive cooking) and returning to a diet closer to that of our origins. His work, though controversial, has inspired many practitioners and patients. It echoes the mitocentric approach by underlining the impact of diet on the biological terrain and proposing a strategy of global restoration.
Palmblad & Kjeldsen-Kragh – Fasting and Rheumatoid Arthritis (1991)

This pioneering study showed that fasting could improve polyarthritis by reducing systemic inflammation. Although focused on an autoimmune disease, it paved the way for the use of fasting as a therapeutic strategy in other conditions. It confirms the idea that metabolic breaks are essential for restoring balance and protecting the mitochondria.
Dale Bredesen – The End of Alzheimer’s (2017)

Bredesen proposed a multimodal protocol combining nutrition, exercise, stress management and sleep optimization. His work showed that some early cases of Alzheimer’s could be reversed through an integrative approach. Although criticized for its methodology, it illustrates the power of combined strategies and is in keeping with the Family Clinic philosophy.
Family Clinic – Cooking to Heal (2026), 200 Hypotoxic Recipes for Every Day

These books form the practical foundation of the Family Clinic approach. They offer recipes adapted to the metabolic terrain, designed to reduce inflammation, protect the mitochondria and restore energy flexibility. They translate theoretical concepts into concrete tools for patients’ everyday lives.
Opening toward the Family Clinic protocol
The Family Clinic protocol is based on combining the contributions of conventional medicine with metabolic strategies. It offers:

items: Hypotoxic nutrition: eliminating pro-inflammatory foods and adopting recipes adapted to the terrain.
Metabolic breaks: intermittent fasting, deep rest, optimized sleep.
Suitable physical activity: stimulating the use of lactate and improving insulin sensitivity.
Stress management: relaxation techniques, meditation, conscious breathing.
Therapeutic integration: judicious use of medications, gradual deprescribing, coordination with metabolic strategies.

blocks.text: This protocol is part of an integrative vision of health in which restoring the biological terrain is the priority. The aim is not to replace conventional medicine, but to complement it and go beyond it, by offering the patient comprehensive and lasting care.
